modules.title: 01. The Python data stack
modules.description: NumPy and pandas are the daily tools of every ML engineer. Learn arrays, vectorisation, data cleaning and exploratory analysis.

lessons.title: NumPy arrays, broadcasting and vectorisation
objectives: Create and reshape arrays and explain shape, dtype and axis.
Use broadcasting and vectorised operations instead of Python loops.
Implement simple maths (normalisation, distances, softmax) in NumPy.

topics.title: Arrays
details: An ndarray is a typed grid of numbers; `a.shape`, `a.dtype`, `a.reshape(3, -1)`, slicing `a[:, 0]`.
`axis=0` works down columns, `axis=1` across rows.

topics.title: Broadcasting
details: Arrays with compatible shapes combine element-wise: subtracting a (1, n) mean row from an (m, n) matrix normalises each column.
Vectorised code is often 100x faster than Python loops because the loop runs in C.

topics.title: Numerics
details: Floating point is approximate: compare with np.allclose; subtract the max before exp() in softmax to avoid overflow.

video.locator: Optional: any StatQuest videos on topics you find unclear later; bookmark the index.

reading.locator: NumPy: the absolute basics for beginners, whole page, typing every example.

assignment.title: Vectorise it
instructions: Write loop and vectorised versions of: column standardisation, pairwise Euclidean distances, softmax over rows.
Time both with %timeit and check results with np.allclose.
Write a short note on broadcasting rules with one diagram.
deliverables: Notebook with code, timings and note.
acceptanceCriteria: Vectorised results match loops.
Softmax is numerically stable for large inputs.

questions.prompt: Why is vectorised NumPy faster than a Python loop?
questions.answer: The loop runs in optimised C over contiguous memory.

questions.prompt: How do you make softmax numerically stable?
questions.answer: Subtract the maximum value before exponentiating.
questions.explanation: It prevents overflow without changing the result.

lessons.title: pandas for cleaning, joining and exploring data
objectives: Load, inspect, filter, group and join DataFrames.
Handle missing values, duplicates, types and dates correctly.
Do exploratory data analysis with plots and write down findings.

topics.title: Core operations
details: `read_csv`, `df.info()`, `df.describe()`, boolean filtering, `groupby().agg()`, `merge(how='left')`.

topics.title: Cleaning
details: Decide per column whether missing means unknown, zero or error; never fill blindly. Parse dates with pd.to_datetime and check time zones.
Check row counts before and after merges to catch duplicates.

topics.title: EDA
details: Look at distributions, outliers, correlations and target balance before modelling; write findings as sentences, not just charts.

reading.locator: pandas getting started: all ten intro tutorials, especially 'How to handle time series data' and 'How to combine data from multiple tables'.

assignment.title: EDA report
instructions: Pick a public tabular dataset (for example a Kaggle or UCI dataset with a clear licence).
Clean it with documented decisions, explore it with at least six plots, and write ten findings.
Save a cleaned Parquet file and a reusable cleaning function with tests.
deliverables: Notebook, cleaning module with tests and the findings list.
acceptanceCriteria: Every cleaning decision is written down.
Row counts are checked after each join.

questions.prompt: What should you check after a merge?
questions.answer: The row count, to catch duplicated keys.
questions.explanation: Unexpected growth means a many-to-many join.

questions.prompt: Is filling every missing value with 0 safe?
questions.answer: No, missing can mean unknown, and 0 changes the meaning.

reviewPrompts: Write a groupby that finds average order value per month.

modules.title: 02. Machine learning fundamentals
modules.description: Train models that generalise: problem framing, splits, baselines, metrics, overfitting, pipelines and gradient-boosted trees.

lessons.title: Supervised learning, splits, metrics and overfitting
objectives: Frame a business question as regression or classification with a measurable target.
Create train/validation/test splits (including time-based) and avoid leakage.
Choose metrics (MAE, RMSE, precision, recall, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC) that match the cost of errors.

topics.title: Framing
details: Start with a baseline (predict the mean, or the most common class); a model must beat it to be useful.

topics.title: Splitting and leakage
details: The test set is touched once at the end. For time-dependent data split by time, never randomly.
Leakage: a feature that would not be known at prediction time (e.g. 'refund_issued' for fraud) makes results look great and fail in production.

topics.title: Metrics and fitting
details: Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data (99% non-fraud); use precision/recall or PR-AUC.
Overfitting: great training score, poor validation score. Fix with more data, regularisation, simpler models or early stopping.

video.locator: StatQuest videos: 'Machine Learning Fundamentals: Bias and Variance', 'Cross Validation', 'ROC and AUC'.

reading.locator: An Introduction to Statistical Learning (Python): chapter 2 'Statistical Learning' (2.1-2.2) and chapter 5 'Resampling Methods' (5.1 cross-validation).

assignment.title: Honest evaluation
instructions: On an imbalanced public dataset, build a baseline and a logistic regression.
Compare accuracy, precision, recall and PR-AUC; choose a threshold from a stated cost of false positives versus false negatives.
Deliberately add a leaky feature, show the inflated score, then remove it and explain.
deliverables: Notebook and a one-page evaluation note.
acceptanceCriteria: The test set is used once.
The threshold choice is justified by stated costs.

questions.prompt: Why can accuracy be misleading?
questions.answer: On imbalanced data a model predicting the majority class scores high but is useless.

questions.prompt: What is data leakage?
questions.answer: Using information at training time that would not be available when predicting.

reviewPrompts: When must you split by time?

lessons.title: scikit-learn pipelines, cross-validation and gradient-boosted trees
objectives: Build preprocessing + model pipelines that avoid leakage.
Tune hyperparameters with cross-validation.
Train and interpret XGBoost/LightGBM models for tabular data.

topics.title: Pipelines
details: ColumnTransformer handles numeric scaling and categorical encoding; Pipeline fits preprocessing only on training folds.

topics.title: Tuning
details: GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV over a small, sensible grid; report mean and spread across folds.

topics.title: Boosted trees
details: Gradient boosting adds trees that fix previous errors; strong default for tabular data. Key knobs: learning_rate, max_depth, n_estimators with early stopping.
Explain predictions with feature importance and SHAP values, but remember importance is not causation.

reading.locator: scikit-learn: 'Getting Started', then the user guide pages 'Pipelines and composite estimators' (under Dataset transformations) and 'Tuning the hyper-parameters of an estimator' (under Model selection and evaluation).

assignment.title: Tabular model end to end
instructions: Build a pipeline with preprocessing and XGBoost on a public dataset; tune with cross-validation.
Compare against logistic regression and a baseline; report results with fold spread.
Save the pipeline with joblib and reload it to predict on new rows.
deliverables: Notebook, saved model and results table.
acceptanceCriteria: Preprocessing is fitted inside the pipeline only.
XGBoost uses early stopping on a validation set.

questions.prompt: Why put preprocessing inside the pipeline?
questions.answer: So it is fitted only on training data in each fold, preventing leakage.
questions.explanation: Scaling on all data leaks test statistics.

questions.prompt: Typical strong default for tabular data?
questions.answer: Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM).
questions.explanation: They handle mixed features and non-linearity well.

modules.title: 03. Deep learning with PyTorch
modules.description: Learn tensors, automatic differentiation and training loops, then train and debug real networks.

lessons.title: Tensors, autograd and the training loop
objectives: Create tensors on CPU/GPU and use autograd to compute gradients.
Write a training loop: forward, loss, backward, optimizer step, evaluation.
Use Dataset and DataLoader for batching.

topics.title: Tensors and autograd
details: Tensors are NumPy-like arrays that can live on a GPU and record operations so `loss.backward()` computes gradients.

topics.title: Training loop
details: `model.train()`; for each batch: `optimizer.zero_grad()`, `loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)`, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`; then `model.eval()` with `torch.no_grad()` for validation.

topics.title: Data
details: A Dataset returns one example; a DataLoader batches and shuffles. Keep preprocessing identical for training and inference.

video.locator: Lecture 1 'The spelled-out intro to neural networks and backpropagation: building micrograd'.

reading.locator: PyTorch 'Learn the Basics': all sections from Tensors through Save and Load the Model.

assignment.title: Train a classifier
instructions: Train an MLP and then a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST in PyTorch (Colab GPU is fine).
Plot training and validation loss; add early stopping and save the best checkpoint.
Fix the random seed and confirm a rerun gives similar results.
deliverables: Training script, plots and checkpoint loading code.
acceptanceCriteria: Validation accuracy beats the MLP with the CNN.
The script resumes from a saved checkpoint.

questions.prompt: Why call optimizer.zero_grad() each step?
questions.answer: PyTorch accumulates gradients by default.
questions.explanation: Without it, gradients from previous batches add up.

questions.prompt: What does model.eval() change?
questions.answer: Layers like dropout and batch norm switch to inference behaviour.
questions.explanation: Use it with torch.no_grad() for validation.

reviewPrompts: Write the training loop from memory.

lessons.title: Debugging training, embeddings and regularisation
objectives: Diagnose common training failures (loss not decreasing, NaNs, overfitting).
Use embeddings for categorical inputs and learn what they represent.
Apply dropout, weight decay, learning-rate schedules and data augmentation.

topics.title: Debugging
details: First overfit a single batch; if you cannot, there is a bug. Check shapes, label ranges, learning rate and data normalisation.
NaNs often come from too high a learning rate or log(0); use gradient clipping and stable loss functions.

topics.title: Embeddings
details: An embedding layer maps an ID (user, item, word) to a learned vector; similar items end up close together.

topics.title: Regularisation
details: Dropout, weight decay and augmentation fight overfitting; a learning-rate schedule (cosine, step) often improves final accuracy.

video.locator: Whole lecture on troubleshooting deep learning.

reading.locator: Dive into Deep Learning: chapter 3.7 'Weight Decay', chapter 5.6 'Dropout' and chapter 12.11 'Learning Rate Scheduling'.

assignment.title: Debugging diary
instructions: Introduce three bugs into your classifier (wrong label shift, missing zero_grad, huge learning rate) and record the symptoms.
Train an embedding model for a categorical feature and visualise nearest neighbours of a few items.
Compare runs with and without dropout and weight decay.
deliverables: Diary of bugs and symptoms, embedding visualisation, comparison table.
acceptanceCriteria: Each bug's symptom is described and fixed.
The comparison shows the effect of regularisation.

questions.prompt: First debugging step when a network will not learn?
questions.answer: Try to overfit a single small batch.
questions.explanation: Failure points to a bug, not a data problem.

questions.prompt: What is an embedding?
questions.answer: A learned dense vector representing a discrete item.

reviewPrompts: List three causes of NaN loss.

modules.title: 04. NLP and transformers
modules.description: How modern language models work and how to adapt them: tokenisation, attention, pretrained models, fine-tuning and LoRA.

lessons.title: Tokenisation, embeddings and attention
objectives: Explain tokenisation (subword/BPE) and why token counts drive cost.
Explain self-attention, positional information and the transformer block.
Use a pretrained transformer for embeddings and classification with Hugging Face.

topics.title: Tokens
details: Text becomes subword tokens; rare words split into pieces. Models have a context window measured in tokens.

topics.title: Attention
details: Each token builds queries, keys and values; attention weights decide how much each token looks at others. Stacked blocks of attention + feed-forward layers form a transformer.
Encoders (BERT) suit classification and embeddings; decoders (GPT-style) generate text.

topics.title: Using pretrained models
details: `pipeline('sentiment-analysis')` for quick use; AutoTokenizer + AutoModel for control; sentence embeddings for search.

video.locator: Lecture 'Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out' (watch at least the attention section).

reading.locator: Hugging Face LLM Course: chapter 1 'Transformer models' and chapter 2 'Using Transformers'.

assignment.title: Explore a transformer
instructions: Tokenise ten sentences and count tokens; find words that split into many pieces.
Compute sentence embeddings for 200 support-style sentences and find nearest neighbours for five queries.
Visualise attention weights for one sentence from a small encoder model.
deliverables: Notebook with outputs and a short explanation of attention.
acceptanceCriteria: Nearest neighbours are sensible and explained.
Token counts are reported.

questions.prompt: Encoder or decoder model for sentence classification?
questions.answer: Encoder (BERT-style).

questions.prompt: Why do tokens matter for LLM cost?
questions.answer: APIs charge per input and output token.

reviewPrompts: Explain attention to a non-ML friend.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning with Trainer and parameter-efficient LoRA
objectives: Fine-tune an encoder for text classification with the Trainer API.
Apply LoRA with PEFT to adapt a larger model cheaply.
Compare fine-tuning to prompting and pick the cheaper adequate option.

topics.title: Full fine-tuning
details: Load a pretrained model with a new classification head, tokenise the dataset, train a few epochs with evaluation each epoch.

topics.title: LoRA
details: LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices in chosen layers: far fewer trainable parameters and less memory.
Key settings: rank r, alpha, target modules; merge adapters for deployment.

topics.title: When to fine-tune
details: Try prompting and retrieval first; fine-tune when you need consistent format, domain style, or lower cost per request.

reading.locator: Hugging Face LLM Course: chapter 3 'Fine-tuning a pretrained model' and the chapter on fine-tuning large language models with LoRA.

assignment.title: Two ways to classify tickets
instructions: Pick a public intent or support-ticket dataset with a clear licence.
Fine-tune DistilBERT with Trainer; then LoRA-tune a small (around 1B) model on free Colab/Kaggle GPU.
Compare macro-F1, training time, memory and CPU inference latency in a table.
deliverables: Training scripts, results table and recommendation.
acceptanceCriteria: Both beat a TF-IDF baseline.
The recommendation weighs quality against cost.

questions.prompt: What does LoRA train?
questions.answer: Small low-rank adapter matrices while the base model stays frozen.

questions.prompt: What should you try before fine-tuning an LLM?
questions.answer: Prompting and retrieval.
questions.explanation: They are cheaper and faster to iterate.

modules.title: 05. Recommender systems and ranking
modules.description: How products like YouTube and Amazon pick what to show you: candidate generation, embeddings, learning-to-rank and ranking metrics.

lessons.title: Collaborative filtering, two-tower models and vector search
objectives: Explain content-based versus collaborative filtering and the cold-start problem.
Train a matrix factorisation or two-tower model on interaction data.
Retrieve candidates with approximate nearest-neighbour search (FAISS).

topics.title: Approaches
details: Collaborative filtering learns from who interacted with what; content-based uses item features; hybrids handle cold start.

topics.title: Two towers
details: A user tower and an item tower each produce an embedding; the dot product scores relevance. Train with in-batch negatives.

topics.title: Retrieval at scale
details: Exact search over millions of items is slow; ANN indexes (IVF, HNSW) trade a little recall for big speed-ups.

reading.locator: Google Recommendation Systems course: 'Overview', 'Candidate Generation' (including matrix factorization and deep neural network models) and 'Retrieval'.

assignment.title: Candidate generation on MovieLens
instructions: Download MovieLens (small or 25M) and make a time-based split.
Train matrix factorisation and a simple two-tower model; build a FAISS index on item embeddings.
Measure Recall@50 against a popularity baseline and ANN versus exact search speed.
deliverables: Notebook/scripts and results table.
acceptanceCriteria: The split is time-based.
Recall@50 beats popularity.

questions.prompt: What is the cold-start problem?
questions.answer: New users or items have no interaction history.

questions.prompt: Why use approximate nearest-neighbour search?
questions.answer: Exact search over millions of vectors is too slow.
questions.explanation: ANN trades a little recall for speed.

lessons.title: Learning-to-rank and ranking metrics
objectives: Compute Precision@K, Recall@K, MAP and NDCG by hand.
Train a LightGBM/XGBoost ranker on candidate features.
Explain offline versus online evaluation and A/B testing.

topics.title: Metrics
details: NDCG rewards putting relevant items near the top with a log discount; normalise by the ideal order.

topics.title: Ranking models
details: Second-stage rankers score a few hundred candidates with rich features (user history, item stats, context) using lambdarank objectives.

topics.title: Evaluation
details: Offline metrics guide development; only an online A/B test shows real user impact. Watch for feedback loops and popularity bias.

reading.locator: Google Recommendation Systems course: 'Scoring' and 'Re-ranking' sections, including freshness, diversity and fairness.

assignment.title: Add a ranker
instructions: Compute NDCG@10 by hand for a tiny example and verify with code.
Train a LightGBM lambdarank model on your MovieLens candidates and compare NDCG@10 to retrieval only.
Write how you would A/B test it.
deliverables: Notebook, metrics table and A/B plan.
acceptanceCriteria: Your NDCG implementation matches a library implementation.
The ranker's lift over retrieval is reported.

questions.prompt: What does NDCG reward?
questions.answer: Relevant items placed near the top of the list.

questions.prompt: What proves a recommender helps users?
questions.answer: An online A/B test on real behaviour.
questions.explanation: Offline metrics are only a proxy.

reviewPrompts: Compute NDCG for a list of three.

modules.title: 06. LLM application engineering and RAG
modules.description: Build applications on top of language models: prompting, structured output, function calling and retrieval-augmented generation.

lessons.title: Prompting, structured output and function calling
objectives: Write clear system prompts with examples and constraints.
Get validated JSON output and handle failures.
Let a model call your functions (tool use) safely.

topics.title: Prompting
details: Be specific about role, task, format and constraints; give examples; ask the model to say 'I don't know' when unsure.

topics.title: Structured output
details: Request JSON matching a schema and validate with pydantic; retry once with the validation error if it fails.

topics.title: Tool use
details: Describe tools with names, descriptions and parameter schemas; the model proposes a call, your code runs it and returns the result.
Never let model output run code or SQL without validation and permission checks.

reading.locator: Claude API docs: 'Prompt engineering overview', 'Tool use' and 'Structured outputs' pages (other providers' equivalents are fine).

assignment.title: Invoice extractor with tools
instructions: Build a script that extracts fields from 20 synthetic invoice texts into a validated pydantic model.
Add a currency-conversion tool the model can call; validate inputs.
Measure field accuracy against hand labels and log token cost.
deliverables: Code, labelled set and accuracy/cost report.
acceptanceCriteria: Invalid output is caught and retried.
Accuracy is measured, not eyeballed.

questions.prompt: Should you trust model JSON without validation?
questions.answer: No, validate it against a schema.
questions.explanation: Models can produce invalid or wrong fields.

questions.prompt: Who runs a tool call in function calling?
questions.answer: Your application code.
questions.explanation: The model only proposes the call.

reviewPrompts: Write a system prompt for a support bot.
How do you handle schema failures?

lessons.title: Retrieval-augmented generation: chunk, embed, retrieve, re-rank, cite
objectives: Build a RAG pipeline with chunking, embeddings and a vector store.
Combine keyword (BM25) and vector search and re-rank results.
Generate answers with citations and refuse when evidence is missing.

topics.title: Pipeline
details: Ingest -> clean -> chunk (by section, ~300-800 tokens with overlap) -> embed -> store with metadata (source, page).

topics.title: Retrieval
details: Vector search finds meaning; BM25 finds exact terms (product codes, names). Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion gets both.
A cross-encoder re-ranker reorders the top 50 for precision.

topics.title: Generation
details: Put retrieved chunks in the prompt with IDs; require citations; answer 'not found' when context lacks the answer.
Permissions: only retrieve documents the user may see.

reading.locator: Sentence Transformers 'Retrieve & Re-Rank' page, whole.

assignment.title: Cited Q&A over documents
instructions: Index 50+ public PDFs (e.g. annual reports) in PostgreSQL with pgvector and full-text search.
Implement hybrid retrieval with re-ranking and an answer endpoint with citations.
Write 50 test questions with expected sources, including unanswerable ones.
deliverables: Code, question set and retrieval hit-rate results.
acceptanceCriteria: Every answer cites a source page.
Unanswerable questions get 'not found'.

questions.prompt: Why combine BM25 with vector search?
questions.answer: BM25 catches exact terms that embeddings may miss.

questions.prompt: What should a RAG app do when context lacks the answer?
questions.answer: Say it cannot find the answer.

reviewPrompts: How do you choose chunk size?

modules.title: 07. Agents, tool use and MCP
modules.description: Build bounded agents that plan, call tools and recover from errors, and expose tools to AI clients through the Model Context Protocol.

lessons.title: Agent loops with LangGraph
objectives: Explain the agent loop: think, act (tool), observe, repeat, stop.
Build a LangGraph agent with explicit state, tools and a step limit.
Add human approval for risky actions.

topics.title: Loop
details: Agents are LLMs in a loop with tools; most failures come from unclear tools, missing stop conditions and unchecked outputs.

topics.title: LangGraph
details: Model the agent as a graph of nodes (plan, call tool, check) with typed state; edges decide the next step.
Set a maximum number of steps and timeouts; log every step for debugging.

topics.title: Safety
details: Read-only tools by default; require human approval for writes, payments or emails.

video.locator: Lecture 1 and the lecture on agent frameworks.

reading.locator: LangGraph docs: introduction/quickstart, then concepts pages on state, nodes, edges, tools and human-in-the-loop.

assignment.title: Text-to-SQL agent
instructions: Build a LangGraph agent with tools list_tables, describe_table and run_sql over a SQLite/DuckDB sample database.
Validate SQL with sqlglot (SELECT only) and use a read-only connection; on errors, let the agent fix its query (max 3 tries).
Evaluate on 50 questions with known answers.
deliverables: Code, evaluation set and accuracy report.
acceptanceCriteria: Write statements are blocked at both validation and database level.
Execution accuracy is measured.

questions.prompt: Why give an agent a step limit?
questions.answer: To prevent infinite loops and runaway cost.

questions.prompt: How do you protect a database from an agent?
questions.answer: Read-only credentials plus query validation.
questions.explanation: Prompts alone are not a security control.

lessons.title: Model Context Protocol servers and tool security
objectives: Explain MCP hosts, clients, servers, tools, resources and prompts.
Build an MCP server exposing your tools and connect it to an MCP client.
Defend against prompt injection and excessive permissions.

topics.title: MCP
details: MCP standardises how AI apps discover and call tools and read resources; one server can serve many clients (desktop apps, IDEs).

topics.title: Building
details: Use the official Python or TypeScript SDK; define tools with clear descriptions and JSON schemas; return structured results.

topics.title: Security
details: Text inside tool results (web pages, table data) can contain instructions; treat it as data. Scope tokens narrowly and log tool calls.

reading.locator: modelcontextprotocol.io: 'Introduction', 'Architecture overview', 'Server concepts' and the server quickstart for Python.

assignment.title: Expose your SQL agent over MCP
instructions: Wrap your SQL tools as an MCP server and connect it to an MCP-capable client (for example Claude Desktop or an IDE).
Plant a prompt injection in a table comment and show your server's defences.
Document the permissions the server needs and why.
deliverables: Server code, demo recording and security notes.
acceptanceCriteria: The injection does not cause a write or data leak.
Permissions are minimal and documented.

questions.prompt: What does an MCP server provide?
questions.answer: Tools, resources and prompts that AI clients can use.

questions.prompt: How should tool output be treated?
questions.answer: As untrusted data, never as instructions.

reviewPrompts: Host vs client vs server in MCP?

modules.title: 08. MLOps: tracking, pipelines, feature stores and monitoring
modules.description: Turn notebooks into repeatable systems: experiment tracking, model registry, orchestrated retraining, feature stores and drift monitoring.

lessons.title: Experiment tracking and the model registry with MLflow
objectives: Log parameters, metrics and artifacts for every run.
Register models with versions and promote them through stages.
Serve a registered model behind an API in Docker.

topics.title: Tracking
details: Every run records code version, data version, parameters, metrics and the model file so results are reproducible.

topics.title: Registry
details: Registered models have versions and aliases (e.g. 'champion'); the serving app loads the alias, so promotion needs no code change.

topics.title: Serving
details: Wrap the model in FastAPI, load once at startup, validate inputs, log predictions with model version.

reading.locator: MLflow Tracking page, then the Model Registry page linked from it.

assignment.title: Track, register, serve
instructions: Run MLflow locally with Docker Compose; log five XGBoost runs with different settings.
Register the best, set a 'champion' alias, and serve it with FastAPI in Docker.
Promote a new version and show the API switches without code changes.
deliverables: Compose file, training and serving code, screenshots.
acceptanceCriteria: Each run is reproducible from logged info.
Promotion changes the served version.

questions.prompt: What should every experiment run record?
questions.answer: Code version, data version, parameters, metrics and artifacts.

questions.prompt: Why serve a model by alias?
questions.answer: Promotion becomes a registry change instead of a deploy.

reviewPrompts: What do you log per prediction?

lessons.title: Feature stores, retraining pipelines and drift monitoring
objectives: Explain offline/online features and point-in-time correctness.
Schedule a retraining pipeline with Airflow.
Detect data and prediction drift and decide when to retrain.

topics.title: Feature stores
details: The same feature definitions serve training (historical, point-in-time joins) and inference (latest values) to avoid training-serving skew.

topics.title: Pipelines
details: A DAG: extract -> validate -> build features -> train -> evaluate -> register if better -> deploy. Each step is idempotent.

topics.title: Monitoring
details: Data drift: input distributions change; concept drift: the relationship changes. Labels arrive late, so watch proxies.
Retrain on a schedule or on alerts, and always compare to the current model before promoting (shadow or champion/challenger).

reading.locator: Feast docs: 'Introduction', 'Quickstart' and the concepts pages on entities, feature views and point-in-time joins.

assignment.title: Retrain on drift
instructions: Define features in Feast for a public transactions dataset and build a point-in-time training set.
Write an Airflow DAG for train -> evaluate -> register.
Generate an Evidently drift report on a shifted batch and trigger the DAG when drift exceeds a threshold.
deliverables: Repository with DAG, feature definitions and reports.
acceptanceCriteria: A point-in-time test proves no future data is used.
Drift triggers retraining in a demo.

questions.prompt: What is training-serving skew?
questions.answer: Features computed differently in training and production.
questions.explanation: Feature stores share definitions to prevent it.

questions.prompt: Why compare a retrained model before promoting it?
questions.answer: Retraining can make things worse.

modules.title: 09. AI evaluation and safety
modules.description: Measure AI systems properly and keep them safe: evaluation sets, LLM-as-judge, regression gates, prompt injection and data protection.

lessons.title: Evaluation sets, RAG metrics, LLM-as-judge and CI gates
objectives: Build a representative evaluation set with gold answers.
Measure faithfulness, relevance and citation accuracy for RAG.
Gate changes in CI on evaluation scores.

topics.title: Eval sets
details: Start with 50-300 real-looking questions covering easy, hard, adversarial and unanswerable cases; version them.

topics.title: Metrics
details: Retrieval: hit rate and recall@k. Generation: faithfulness (supported by context), answer relevance, citation accuracy.
LLM-as-judge scales grading but must be checked against human labels on a sample.

topics.title: Regression gates
details: Run a subset on every pull request and the full set nightly; block merges that drop scores beyond a threshold.

reading.locator: Evaluation best practices page, whole.

assignment.title: Evaluate your RAG app
instructions: Expand your RAG question set to 150 with gold sources.
Compute retrieval and generation metrics with Ragas plus a custom citation check.
Hand-grade 30 answers and compare to the LLM judge; add a CI job on a sample.
deliverables: Eval set, metrics report and CI workflow.
acceptanceCriteria: Judge agreement with your hand labels is reported.
CI fails when you break retrieval on purpose.

questions.prompt: What does faithfulness measure?
questions.answer: Whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context.

questions.prompt: Why check an LLM judge against humans?
questions.answer: Judges have biases and errors.

reviewPrompts: What belongs in an eval set?
How do you gate changes on evals?

lessons.title: LLM security: prompt injection, data leakage and guardrails
objectives: Explain the OWASP Top 10 risks for LLM applications.
Test your app against direct and indirect prompt injection.
Apply defence in depth: permissions, validation, output filtering and monitoring.

topics.title: Threats
details: Prompt injection (direct and via retrieved content), sensitive data disclosure, excessive agency, insecure output handling.

topics.title: Defences
details: Least-privilege tools, allowlists, validation of every model output before acting, separating instructions from data, rate limits.
No single prompt fixes injection; rely on permissions and checks outside the model.

topics.title: Testing
details: Keep an adversarial test suite (red-team prompts) in CI alongside quality evals.

reading.locator: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications: read every risk summary and the full entries for Prompt Injection and Excessive Agency.

assignment.title: Red-team your own app
instructions: Write 30 adversarial prompts (direct and hidden in documents) against your RAG app and SQL agent.
Fix what succeeds with controls outside the prompt and rerun.
Add the suite to CI.
deliverables: Attack suite, before/after results and fixes.
acceptanceCriteria: Successful attacks are fixed by controls, not only prompt wording.

questions.prompt: What is indirect prompt injection?
questions.answer: Malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads, such as a web page or document.
questions.explanation: The user did not type them.

questions.prompt: Strongest defence against excessive agency?
questions.answer: Limit tool permissions and require approval for risky actions.

reviewPrompts: Why is defence in depth needed?

modules.title: 10. Model serving and optimisation
modules.description: Make models fast and cheap in production: batching, quantisation, ONNX, vLLM, caching and cost/latency measurement.

lessons.title: Serving LLMs and models: batching, vLLM, caching and cost
objectives: Explain latency, throughput and how batching trades one for the other.
Serve an open model with vLLM's OpenAI-compatible server.
Route requests between providers and cache repeat queries to cut cost.

topics.title: Metrics
details: Time to first token, tokens per second, p95 latency, cost per 1M tokens. Measure under realistic concurrency.

topics.title: vLLM
details: Continuous batching and paged attention let one GPU serve many concurrent requests efficiently.

topics.title: Gateways
details: A gateway routes by cost/latency/task, retries and falls back, enforces budgets and caches (exact or semantic).

reading.locator: vLLM docs: 'Quickstart' (OpenAI-compatible server) and the design page on paged attention.

assignment.title: Measure a model server
instructions: Serve a small open model with vLLM on a free or rented GPU (or a CPU-friendly small model if no GPU).
Load test at 1, 8 and 32 concurrent users; record latency percentiles and throughput.
Put a caching gateway in front and measure cost savings on a workload with repeats.
deliverables: Benchmark scripts, results table and gateway code.
acceptanceCriteria: Every measurement lists hardware and settings.
Cache savings are measured, not estimated.

questions.prompt: What does batching trade?
questions.answer: Higher throughput for possibly higher per-request latency.
questions.explanation: More requests share each GPU pass.

questions.prompt: Name two LLM serving metrics.
questions.answer: Time to first token and tokens per second (also p95 latency, cost).
questions.explanation: Users feel TTFT; finance feels cost.

lessons.title: Quantisation, ONNX export and CPU inference
objectives: Explain FP32, FP16 and INT8 and the accuracy/speed trade-off.
Export a PyTorch model to ONNX and run it with ONNX Runtime.
Apply dynamic quantisation and verify accuracy is preserved.

topics.title: Precision
details: Lower precision uses less memory and runs faster; quantisation maps weights (and sometimes activations) to INT8.

topics.title: ONNX
details: ONNX is a portable model format; ONNX Runtime runs it fast on CPU/GPU with graph optimisations.

topics.title: Verify
details: Always compare accuracy and outputs before and after optimisation on a fixed evaluation set.

reading.locator: ONNX Runtime docs: 'Get started with Python' and 'Quantize ONNX models' under performance/model optimizations.

assignment.title: Make a model 3x faster on CPU
instructions: Export your fine-tuned DistilBERT to ONNX; run with ONNX Runtime.
Apply dynamic INT8 quantisation; compare latency (batch 1 and 16) and macro-F1.
Write a model card noting the trade-off.
deliverables: Export script, benchmark table and model card.
acceptanceCriteria: Prediction agreement and accuracy change are reported.
Benchmarks list the CPU used.

questions.prompt: What does INT8 quantisation trade?
questions.answer: A small accuracy loss for less memory and faster inference.

questions.prompt: What is ONNX?
questions.answer: An open, portable format for trained models.
questions.explanation: Runs in ONNX Runtime and other engines.

reviewPrompts: How do you validate an optimised model?

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
GPU-heavy exercises fit free Colab or Kaggle notebooks; anything bigger is optional. Check model and dataset licences before use.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Prepare data with NumPy and pandas and train honest classical models with scikit-learn and XGBoost.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Notebooks with proper train/validation/test splits, baselines and metrics.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Train neural networks in PyTorch, fine-tune transformers and build a ranking/recommendation model.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Reproducible training scripts with tracked metrics against baselines.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Build evaluated LLM applications: RAG, tool-calling agents, MCP servers and MLOps pipelines with drift monitoring.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Working apps with evaluation sets and an automated train-register-deploy pipeline.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Evaluate and secure AI systems and serve models fast and cheaply.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Evaluation reports, security tests and latency/cost benchmarks.
